conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for making time for this today. I’m Dr. Lee, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is simply to check in on how you’re feeling now that your baby has arrived, because the transition to motherhood can bring surprises we don’t always talk about.

We’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually just called the EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question screen that helps us spot signs of depression, anxiety, or distress that can creep up any time in the first postpartum year. There are no right or wrong answers; whatever you share stays between us unless you tell me something that makes me worry about your safety or your baby’s. We’ll go at your pace, and you can pause or skip anything you need to.

I’ll ask each question conversationally—no forms to fill out—and we’ll cover how you’ve felt over the past seven days. Ready to start?

Over the last week, have you still been able to enjoy things that used to make you happy, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

It’s… it’s definitely slipped. I used to love putting on a podcast and baking something simple—banana bread, cookies, whatever—but this week when I even think about pulling out the mixer it just feels like one more chore. Same with the little Netflix show my husband and I would binge; I sit there, but I’m not really laughing. Everything feels kind of gray, like I’m going through the motions but not actually tasting the cookie when I finally take a bite.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes—like if the baby makes a silly face or my husband trips over the diaper bag—I’ll catch myself laughing, but it fades fast. Most of the day I feel too tired or worried to find much funny, so I’d say “not so much” rather than “yes, as much as I used to.”
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I keep thinking, “Tomorrow I’ll feel excited about taking the baby for a walk or grabbing a coffee,” but when the morning comes it just feels… flat. Even little plans—like my sister dropping by—sound exhausting instead of fun.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah... that happens a lot. Like, if the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle her right away, my brain jumps straight to “I’m a terrible mom—she deserves someone who knows what she needs.” Or when I burned the oatmeal last week, I sat on the kitchen floor crying because I told myself I can’t even handle breakfast for my own family. I know, logically, it’s just oatmeal, but in the moment it feels like proof I’m failing.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Most days, yeah. My heart races the second I hear her make a weird grunt in the bassinet, and I’m convinced she’s stopped breathing, so I go poke her foot until she stirs. Or I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly picture her slipping out of my arms on the changing table—images just pop in, even though nothing’s happening. I can usually talk myself down after a few minutes, but it keeps happening all day, even when everything’s calm.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes it hits really fast—like my chest gets tight and I feel I can’t get a deep breath. Yesterday I was just warming a bottle and suddenly pictured her choking, and my hands started shaking so badly I had to set the bottle down and grip the counter. It passes after a minute or two, but those waves of panic come out of nowhere a few times a day.
Things have been getting on top of me

A lot of the time. I’ll be trying to answer one text, the baby starts crying, the dog’s barking at the delivery guy, and I just freeze—like my brain can’t pick which fire to put out first. I end up crying over the kitchen sink because it feels as if everyone needs something and I’m already running on empty. I manage to get through the basics, but it’s like I’m barely one step ahead all day long.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… even when the baby finally settles, my mind won’t shut off. I lie there staring at the ceiling going over every little thing I did wrong that day—did I burp her long enough, did I snap at my husband, why can’t I handle this better—and then I hear her make one tiny noise and I’m wide-awake again. It takes me forever to drift off, and when I do I pop back awake for no clear reason. I’m lucky if I get a three-hour stretch before she’s up to eat.
I have felt sad or miserable

That pretty much sums up most of the week. I’ll be feeding her and tears just start rolling down my face for no real reason. It’s like this heavy cloud that settles in and won’t lift. Some afternoons I end up sobbing in the rocker because everything feels hopeless, even though I know I love her and want to be okay.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s been like that. A few times it’s hit me out of nowhere—yesterday I was just folding her tiny onesies and I just started bawling. Other times it’s when I feel overwhelmed, like if she won’t latch or I’m running late for her check-up. I’d say I end up in tears maybe three, four times this week.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—nothing like that. I get exhausted and cry, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again so I can take care of her.

It sounds like this week has felt overwhelmingly heavy for you-like joy has been replaced by a constant gray fog. You described how even simple pleasures such as baking or watching your favorite show feel flat, and how waves of worry, panic, and self-blame crash over you many times a day. Despite loving your baby deeply, you're exhausted, tearful, and running on empty, yet you still reached out and shared your experience with courage and honesty.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only occasional laughter that quickly fades and overall reduced ability to find things funny, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent anhedonia—anticipation of events feels flat and exhausting, matching 'Hardly at all</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "a lot," with multiple recent examples of harsh self-criticism over minor parenting tasks, matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes intrusive, racing, catastrophic thoughts occurring "most days" and "all day," which aligns with "very often."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic attacks multiple times a day, matching 'Yes, sometimes</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm, inability to prioritize demands, and emotional collapse, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>"most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness, unexpected crying during routine tasks, and hopeless sobbing—semantically equivalent to "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying 3–4 times in the past week, clearly matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 24 (range 0-30) places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. Core symptoms map onto <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood or anhedonia nearly every day (Q1-2 scored 2 & 3), multiple associated features including <sym>self-reproach</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>sleep impairment</sym>, <sym>psychomotor agitation</sym>, <sym>feelings of worthlessness</sym>, and <sym>diminished concentration</sym> (reflected in Q3-8 scores of 3). You also describe <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic attacks</sym>, common in postpartum presentations. Q10 score of 0 indicates no current self-harm ideation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to confirm diagnosis and discuss treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or compatible <med>antidepressant medication</med> safe for breastfeeding
3. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor progress after intervention begins
4. Reach out today to Postpartum Support International (1-800-944-4773, text 800-944-4773 English/971-203-7773 Spanish) for 24/7 support groups and local provider referrals
5. Share these findings with a trusted support person so they can help with baby care, meals, and checking in on you daily
6. Practice small self-care anchors: five-minute outdoor breath of fresh air, accept help with night feeds when offered, and keep water/snacks within reach to stabilize blood sugar
7. Use the 3-minute paced breathing or 5-4-3-2-1 grounding when <sym>panic</sym> rises; place baby in safe spot while you regroup
8. Sleep hygiene: turn off screens 30 min before lying down, use a fan/white-noise to cover household sounds, accept that naps trump chores
9. If mood worsens, self-harm thoughts develop, or you feel unsafe caring for your baby, treat as an emergency-call 988 (US) or go to nearest ED
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Screening Note – Postpartum Depression Screen  

<sym>Depressed mood</sym>: persistent sadness, frequent tearfulness (3–4×/week), anhedonia, loss of pleasure/anticipation.  
<sym>Anxiety symptoms</sym>: near-daily excessive worry, intrusive catastrophic images, episodic panic (chest tightness, trembling), hypervigilance about infant safety.  
<sym>Self-blame/guilt</sym>: recurrent feelings of maternal inadequacy, catastrophizing routine mishaps.  
<sym>Functional overload</sym>: frequent “freezing,” feeling unable to prioritize demands, sense of running “on empty.”  
<sym>Sleep disturbance</sym>: difficulty initiating/maintaining sleep unrelated to infant awakenings, racing thoughts.  
<sym>Risk-related</sym>: denies any self-harm ideation (endorsed “No” to Q10).  

Pattern: symptoms present most days for ≥ past week, interfere with coping and enjoyment of motherhood.  
Screening significance: meets threshold indicators for possible <med>postpartum depression</med> with prominent <med>anxiety</med>; further diagnostic evaluation recommended.
